Macron közölte, a francia belügyminiszter regionális prefektusokkal találkozott, hogy fokozzák az éberséget az orosz hibrid támadásokra adott válaszként. A francia elnök azt mondta, utasította a kormányt, hogy készítsen tervet a kritikus infrastruktúra, valamint a legérzékenyebb védelmi ipari és technológiai létesítmények védelmére, többek között a drón- és kibertámadásokkal szemben. Azt ígérte, hogy Franciaország válaszolni fog az orosz hibrid támadásokra. „Nem hagyjuk magunkat megfélemlíteni, mert tudjuk, hogy ma Ukrajnában a mi biztonságunk forog kockán” – tette hozzá. Donald Tusk lengyel miniszterelnök múlt héten jelentette be, hogy meghiúsítottak egy lengyel határátkelő elleni orosz támadást az ukránok segítségével, egy sajtótájékoztatón pedig azt mondta, közvetlenül az amerikai CIA igazgatójától , John Ratcliffe-től kapott egy „meglehetősen pontos jelentést” a következő hónapokban várható lehetséges fejleményekről. Tusk közölte, arra számít, hogy Oroszország további határátkelők ellen hajt majd végre támadásokat, hogy leállítsák az Ukrajna felé tartó kereskedelmi útvonalakat. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Andy Burnham will meet Donald Trump face-to-face on Tuesday. Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham will meet Donald Trump face-to-face on Tuesday. Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images Donald Trump Analysis Andy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictable Pippa Crerar Political editor PM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy Sun 20 Sep 2026 14.45 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 16.00 EDT Share No international relationship has more power to determine the success of Andy Burnham’s premiership. So you might imagine the stakes for the prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump on Tuesday would be high. Yet Burnham may prove to be a lucky general. The balance of risk has shifted. Trump is unpopular at home, where inflation remains high, and is mired in an intractable conflict in Iran that has the potential to sink his midterm dreams . When Keir Starmer first visited Trump in February 2025, the situation could not have been more different. The notoriously unpredictable president had just won the US election and was at the height of his powers – and was showing muscle on Nato and Ukraine, and with threats of tariffs. Starmer’s “keep calm and carry on” strategy helped keep Trump on board the defence alliance and also protected the UK from the worst of his aggression over trade. But it came with a cost: he was often left looking obsequious and at odds with the national mood. Burnham defended his predecessor’s approach but in June signalled he would take a different direction . “Obviously the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything they say,” he said. “We’ve got in trouble in the past when that happens.” Downing Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister. Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama. Early clues about how the talks might go from the White House perspective have been mixed. In June, Trump suggested Burnham was “extremely liberal” (not as a compliment) and dismissively described him as the “mayor of a town”. The US president remains angry the UK did not join his strikes on Iran, and has attacked the country as a “dying” nation “on the edge of disaster”. More recent comments that he might not help if Argentina again tried to seize the Falklands , and that he would love to see a united Ireland , suggest his displeasure has not abated. But that will not necessarily translate into a strained personal relationship with Burnham. The pair have spoken on the phone twice and are said to have got on. The prime minister’s laid-back, confident style is likely to go down well with Trump, who has already shown with the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani , that he can warm to leftwingers. On policy too, government insiders point to small reasons for hope: Trump responded warmly to reports the UK government was going to “open up” the North Sea (although the decision to drill at two fields has been delayed) and has – so far – been relatively restrained when asked about the UK’s planned West Bank settlement trade ban . Their meeting will be fraught with tension over both matters, and other areas – such as defence spending and the Iran war – have potential for further clashes. It will help Burnham that Tuesday’s talks will be held on the comparatively neutral ground of the UN, rather than at the White House. As such, he will avoid the jeopardy of an Oval Office press conference that Trump could easily derail. Trump may also decide he has had enough fights for one day. His meeting with Burnham will follow his address to the UN. Last year Trump told world leaders their countries were “going to hell” over their immigration policies. The UK meeting may end up as just a sideshow. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Burnham’s views on Trump have also shifted since he took office. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he said the US president would not be welcome in the city, blaming his “poisonous” politics. After winning his seat as an MP in Makerfield, he warned against the “divided, dark politics” of the US. But over the summer, Burnham appeared to shrug off potential divisions, telling reporters that “everyone says things as politicians”. The new prime minister said he would “say what I feel” to Trump but – crucially – would also try to “find a connection” with the mercurial president. Trump claims triumphal arch will serve as a ‘top grade military complex’ to store weapons Read more With Trump now weaker domestically, political power in the US is starting to shift to who comes next. Burnham is walking into the room with a president who is running out of time. Yet Trump is in power for two more years, and he is nothing if not unpredictable. Burnham’s priority may be on domestic affairs, but his closest aides acknowledge that the biggest weight on the UK right now is Trump’s war in Iran. While the war continues to wreak damage on the British economy, Burnham will struggle to deliver his promises of change. So for the time being, the power still rests with Trump, and Burnham may yet find he has to navigate a perilous path as Starmer did before him. UK News Latvian Men Accused of Spying After Allegedly Breaking Into UK Airbase Used by US, NATO Authorities said they found two men inside the airbase late at night after discovering a hole in the outside fence. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print A general view of the entrance to RAF Molesworth in Huntingdon, England, on Oct. 8, 2026. Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images Jill McLaughlin 10/8/2026 | Updated: 10/8/2026 0:00 X 1 UK police arrested two Latvian men on espionage charges after they allegedly broke into the RAF Molesworth airbase, used as a U.S. and NATO intelligence center near London, during the late hours of Oct. 7, authorities announced. Counter Terrorism authorities are looking into why the men were at the airbase, lead investigator Commander Helen Flanagan said. “A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage and enquiries are very much ongoing,” Flanagan said in a statement. Metropolitan police and Cambridgeshire Constabulary officers were checking the perimeter of the airbase Wednesday night when they came across an abandoned vehicle, leading them to investigate the perimeter fence. Officers found a section of fence that had been breached and located two men inside the airbase. The suspects were arrested at 2 a.m. Thursday, according to investigators. The men—ages 32 and 36—were Latvian nationals living in the UK, authorities confirmed. Related Stories UK Makes 7th Arrest Over Security Incident Near RAF Fairford Airbase Vigilance Must Be Permanent: The Fairford Arrests and the Threat to US Assets The men were arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage, and taken to a Cambridge police station. They were later also charged and arrested on suspicion of espionage, police reported. The men remain in custody, according to investigators with the UK’s Counter Terrorism Policing unit, which is investigating the incident. “As ever, I would ask the public to remain vigilant and if you see anything of concern, then to contact police,” Flanagan said. Officers were continuing to carry out searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation, according to police. The abandoned vehicle found at the airbase was also recovered by authorities and taken to a nearby police station. Technicians are searching the vehicle. A car passing potholes in a road near Peterborough in Cambridgeshire, England, on April 4, 2018. Joe Giddens/PA Wire The area around the car was initially blocked off by police but after a review by detectives, the car was cleared, authorities said. The investigation is in its early stages and so far, nothing suggests the incident is connected to events at RAF Fairford last week, Flanagan said. UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting thanked police and security teams for their work in a statement Thursday. “We are highly vigilant about potential threats to our military sites and work closely with the police to keep them secure,” Streeting said in a post on X. “The protection of our bases is multi-layered, including physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, monitoring, and counter-drone capabilities.” Authorities arrested a seventh suspect Tuesday in connection to a security incident at RAF Fairford airbase that occurred Sept. 27. The 22-year-old man, a British national from London, was detained on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. The RAF Fairford incident is suspected by the British government to be tied to an Iranian terrorist plot, and police said Monday they were investigating whether suspects involved were acting for a foreign state. Armed police officers attend a suspected terrorist incident at RAF Fairford airbase in Fairford, England, on Sept. 27, 2026. Toby Shepheard/Reuters The Pentagon pulled all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford after the announcement. The supersonic, long-range heavy bombers belonging to the U.S. Air Force were stationed at the base. No reason was given by the Pentagon for the removal of military assets at the base. RAF Molesworth is a military installation in Cambridgeshire used for joint U.S. and NATO operations, and houses the Joint Intelligence Operations Center Europe Analytic Center, which provides military intelligence and analysis for the U.S. European Command. The base also provides support for the U.S. Air Force. Pentagon officials didn’t immediately return a request for comment about whether they planned to make additional changes after the RAF Molesworth arrests. The Latvian Embassy in London also didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
